sections.content: A headline is compressed, and its conventions are common in the press, not rules of the language. First, the present tense is used for something that has just happened: *Dimite el alcalde* tells you the mayor has resigned. Second, the verb often comes first and the subject follows. Third, a headline may drop articles, or leave out the verb altogether: *Alerta por lluvias en la costa*. Fourth, a colon names who is speaking: *Portavoz: «El puente seguirá cerrado»*. The full sentences of the article itself keep their usual tenses and articles.

sections.title: Headline and full sentence
rows: El alcalde ha dimitido. (present for a past event, verb first)
Arde un almacén en la zona industrial
Un almacén ha empezado a arder en la zona industrial. (present, verb first)
Alerta por lluvias en la costa
Hay una alerta por lluvias en la costa. (no verb, no article)
El portavoz dice que el puente seguirá cerrado. (a colon names the speaker)

items.english: The mayor resigns. (the resignation has happened)

items.spanish: Alerta por lluvias en la costa
Arde un almacén en la zona industrial
items.english: Warehouse on fire in the industrial zone.

sections.content: English headlines also use the present for the past, so this will feel familiar. The mistake is to carry headline style into ordinary writing: in the body of an article, and in your own sentences, keep the full verb forms and the articles (*El alcalde ha dimitido*). Save *Dimite el alcalde* for the headline.
